findings.finding: Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for distinct a+b+c=n. For n multiple of 6, choose (d,2d,3d) → lcm=6d=n, giving minimal possible lcm=n. Thus f(n)=n when 6|n; otherwise f(n)>n. Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025!. Since M=3^{2025!}≫2025!, only terms with f(M+c)≥M/2025! give non‑zero floor. For M+c where 6|M+c (i.e., c≡0 mod 6), f=M+c, so floor≈⌊2025!·(M+c)/M⌋≈2025!+⌊2025!·c/M⌋=2025!. For other c, f≫n but still <M, floor=0. Hence g(c)=1 for c≡0 (mod 6), else 0. Sum over given c’s (all ≡0 mod 6) →6·1=6 ⇒ p/q=6/1 ⇒ p+q=7 ⇒ 7 mod 99991=7.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n (distinct). For huge n≈3^k, choose a,b,c as powers of 3; LCM=largest power. Thus f(M+c)≈largest power ≤M (or ≤5M). Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025!≈⌊f(M+c)/M·2025!⌋/2025!. For c small, f(M+c)=M (since 1+3+M‑4?); for 4M, f(5M)=5M. Sum g’s → rational p/q; find (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure distinctness, verify minimal LCM truly equals largest power, handle c values >M.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. For n≥9, f(n)≤n (always ≤n, never >n except n=8). Hence for huge M=3^{2025!}, f(M+c) is either ≤M or slightly >M but ≤2M.  

Let N=2025!. Then g(c)=⌊N·f(M+c)/M⌋/N = k/N where k∈{0,…,2N}. Since f(M+c)/M∈[0,2], k≈N·(f/M).  

Because f(M+c)≤M for all c (except possibly tiny cases), N·f/M ≤N, so k≤N. Moreover f(M+c)≥M? Actually for most n, minimal LCM equals n (when n multiple of 6) → f(M+c)=M+c≈M, giving k=N (since (N·M)/M=N). For n not multiple of 6, f<M, giving k<N.  

Thus g(c)=1 when M+c is a multiple of 6, else g(c)=0 (since floor(N·f/M) is either N or <N, and division by N yields 1 or <1; but any value <1 is a fraction with denominator N, and sum of six such terms will be integer + fraction <6/N≈0).  

Check c values: compute (M+c) mod 6. Since M=3^{N} is odd, 3^{odd}≡3 (mod 6). So M≡3 (mod 6). Then M+c≡3+c (mod 6).  

c list: 0→3 (≠0), 4M→4·3≡0 (mod 6) → g=1, 1848374≡? 1848374 mod 6 = 1848374‑6·308062=1848374‑1848372=2 → 3+2=5≠0 →0.  
10162574 mod 6 = 10162574‑6·1693762=10162574‑10162572=2 →0.  
265710644 mod 6 = 4 →3+4=1→0.  
44636594 mod 6 = 2 →3+2=5→0.  

Thus sum = 1. So p/q=1/1 ⇒ p+q=2. 2 mod 99991 = 2.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Global min ratio LCM/sum =6/11 (triplet 2,3,6); next possible ratio =4/7 (1,2,4). Thus f(N)=6/11·N when N≡0 (mod 11); otherwise f(N)≥4/7·N, and equality holds for N≡0 (mod 7).  

M=3^{2025!} ⇒ M≡? (mod 11,7). Compute M mod 11,7 (use 3^{2025!} cycles). For each c given, N=M+c. Determine if N≡0 (mod 11) → ratio 6/11, else if N≡0 (mod 7) → ratio 4/7, else larger (but c’s chosen make one of these true). Since 7,11|2025!, denominators divide 2025! ⇒ g(c)=f(N)/N exactly (no floor loss). Sum g’s = Σ (p_i/q_i) with q_i∈{7,11}. Reduce to p/q, compute (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure N’s congruences; verify no other lower ratios exist; handle cases where N not multiple of 7 or 11 (not needed here).

Insights: f(N)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=N ⇒ use 1+d+e=N ⇒ d|e ⇒ d|N−1. So f(N)=(N−1)*(p−1)/p where p=smallest odd prime divisor of N−1.  
Thus g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025! = (p−1)/p if p≤2025, else =⌊2025!·(p−1)/p⌋/2025!.  
Compute p for each c: c=0→p=5; 4M→p>2025; 1848374→p=11; 10162574→p>2025; 265710644→p=29; 44636594→p=17.  
All terms have denominator 2025!; sum = N/2025!. Reduce by d=gcd(N,2025!). Finally compute (N/d)+(2025!/d) mod 99991. (Key pitfall: ensure p=3 never divides N−1; handle p>2025 via floor).

Insights: f(n) = n·(2/3)(1‑k/d) where d is the smallest divisor ≥7, d≢0 (mod 3), d≠8; k=1 if d≡1, k=2 if d≡2. For d≤2025, 3^{2025!}≡1 (mod d). So M≡1 (mod d). Test each c: n=M+c ≡1+c (mod d). Find smallest allowed d dividing n. Compute f(n)=n·(2/3)(1‑k/d). Then g(c)=⌊2025!·f/M⌋/2025! = (f/M) rounded down to 1/2025! steps. Sum six g’s → rational p/q. Compute p+q mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure d≥7, exclude 8; handle c=4M (c≡0) separately (n=5M). Use d dividing 5M (i.e., d|5). Smallest allowed divisor of 5M is 5? but 5≡2 mod 3 and <7 → invalid, next is 7 (doesn’t divide). So use d=10? etc. Verify each case.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Minimal ratio lcm/n is 6/11, attained iff 11|n (triple 2t,3t,6t). For any n, f(n)=⌈6n/11⌉ when 11∤n? Actually f(n)≥⌈6n/11⌉ and equals 6n/11 for 11|n. Since M≡1 (mod 11) and all c give n≡1,5,2,3 (mod 11) → none divisible by 11. Thus f(M+c)≈⌈6(M+c)/11⌉. Then g(c)=⌊2025!·⌈6(M+c)/11⌉/M⌋/2025!≈⌊2025!·6/11⌋/2025! (c‑terms negligible). Compute K=⌊2025!·6/11⌋. Sum of six g’s =6K/2025!. Reduce p/q, then output (p+q) mod 99991. (Key: use 6/11 ratio, M≡1 (mod 11), c≪M, floor unaffected.)

Insights: f(n)=min_{a<b<c, a+b+c=n}LCM(a,b,c)=n·min_{S|n}r(S) where r(S)=ab/(ab+a+b) for coprime pair (a,b) giving smallest LCM; optimal pairs are (2,b). Then S_b=(ab+a+b)/gcd(2,b)= (3b+2)/gcd(2,b) (≡7,11,17,…). r(b)=2b/(3b+2). Since M=3^{2025!}, for any S_b (≠multiple of 3) we have M≡1 (mod S_b) (φ(S_b)≤2025! ⇒3^{2025!}≡1). Thus M+c divisible by S_b ⇔ S_b|c+1. For each c, find smallest b≥3 with S_b|c+1; then f(M+c)= (M+c)·r(b). If none, f≈M+c (ratio≈1). Compute g(c)=⌊2025!·f/M⌋/2025! = r(b)+⌊2025!·r(b)·c/M⌋/2025! (second term zero unless c multiple of M). Use c values: 0,4M,1848374,10162574,265710644,44636594. Only 4M gives extra integer term. Sum g’s → rational p/q; output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure S_b not divisible by 3, use M≡1 mod S_b; handle case no divisor (ratio ≈1). Use b‑search up to needed S (c+1≤~3e8). Compute r(b) as reduced fraction. Finally compute p+q mod 99991.

Insights: f(n)=min L where ∃a≠b|L, a+b≡n (mod L) and a+b<L. For huge odd N (M+c) we only need tiny L. Test L from 6 upward; check if r=n mod L equals sum of two distinct proper divisors of L. First such L = f(N). Compute k=⌊2025!·L/M⌋ (≈0) → g(c)=k/2025!. Sum six g’s → p/q; reduce; answer (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfall: assume f≈N; actually f often tiny (≤~100). Use modular exponentiation for M=3^{2025!}.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM of three divisors = n·r where r=ab/(ab+a+b) for distinct a,b>1 (with 1 as third divisor). r is smallest possible when N is divisible by K= (ab+a+b)/gcd(ab,ab+a+b).  

For N=M=3^{2025!}: only K=3^t divide N → best pair (3,6) → r=2/3.  

For N=M+c (c≡2 mod 3, c+1 multiple of 5, not of 7,11,…): K=5 divides N (via c+1) → best pair (2,6) → r=3/5.  

For N=5M (c=4M): N divisible by 5 and 3 → K=5 gives r=3/5 (better than 2/3).  

Thus g(0)=2/3, the other five g’s=3/5. Sum=2/3+3=11/3 → p+q=11+3=14.  

Pitfalls: ensure 1 isn’t reused, use K condition (c+1 mod K=0 for K coprime to 3), check all small K; denominator always divides 2025!.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ use 1+d+e=n, so f(n)=min lcm(d,e) where d+e=n‑1 and d|e (or e|d). Hence f(N)= (N‑1)·(p‑1)/p where p=smallest odd prime divisor of S=N‑1.  

For N=M+c (M=3^{2025!}), S=M+c‑1. For odd primes ≤2025, M‑1≡0 (mod p) ⇒ S≡c (mod p). Thus p is the smallest odd prime dividing c (if ≤2025) else the smallest odd prime >2025 dividing S.  

c values give p: 0→5, 1848374→11, 10162574→? (large), 265710644→29, 44636594→17, 4M→11549 (found by search).  

g(c)=⌊2025!·f(N)/M⌋/2025! = (p‑1)/p for p≤2025; for p>2025, g(c)=1‑⌊2025!/p⌋/2025!‑1/2025!.  

Compute sum S=∑g(c) as integer N/2025!; N=2025!·152272/27115 –⌊2025!/11549⌋ –⌊2025!/p₂⌋ –2.  

Find p₂ (smallest odd prime divisor of M+10162574‑1) by testing primes; none ≤1 000 000, so p₂>10⁶.  

Finally p+q = (N+2025!)/gcd(N,2025!). Reduce mod 99991.  

Pitfalls: ensure p for c=0 is 5 (3∤M‑1); handle p>2025 via floor formula; large factorial modulo prime needed only for 2025! mod p. Use Python big ints.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ f(N)/N = min_{d|N} r(d), where r(d) is best ratio for exact sum d. Small‑ratio “primitive” sums (ordered by ratio) are: 11→6/11, 7→4/7, 17→10/17, 10→3/5, 23→14/23, 13→8/13, 5→5/8,… (ratio ↑). For N=M=3^{2025!}, only divisors are powers of 3 ⇒ smallest admissible d=9 ⇒ r=2/3. For N=M+c (c even, c≠0), M≡1 (mod d) for d coprime to 3, so N≡c+1 (mod d). Hence N divisible by d ⇔ d|c+1. Compute c+1 factorization; find smallest primitive d dividing it → gives r. For c=1848374,10162574,265710644,44636594, the minimal d’s are 7, 7, 7, 7 respectively ⇒ r=4/7. For c=4M (N=5M) only divisors 3^a·5 ⇒ best d=9 ⇒ r=2/3. Thus g(c)=r (since 2025! multiple of denominators). Sum S=2/3+2/3+4·(4/7)=4/3+16/7= (28+48)/21=76/21 ⇒ p+q=76+21=97 ⇒ 97 mod 99991 = 97.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Best ratios L/S are from primitive triples: 6/11 (S=11), 4/7 (S=7), 30/47 (S=47), 64/97 (S=97), 110/167 (S=167), 16/25 (S=25). For N=M+c (c≠0) N≡c+1 (mod odd S) and N not divisible by 3, so usable S must divide c+1 and be coprime to 3. Compute c+1 factorizations:  
0→M (only 3‑powers) ⇒ ratio 2/3.  
4M⇒5·3^K (no 7,11) ⇒ ratio 2/3.  
1848374+1=5³·31·53 ⇒ S=25 gives 16/25 (best).  
10162574+1=3²·5²·31²·47 ⇒ S=47 gives 30/47.  
265710644+1=3³·5·97·103·197 ⇒ S=97 gives 64/97.  
44636594+1=3·5·103·167·173 ⇒ S=167 gives 110/167.  

Sum g’s = 2/3+2/3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 224414944/57101475.  
p+q mod 99991 = **41754**.  

Pitfalls: Include only odd S (N not ≡0 (mod 3)); ensure S|c+1; use exact fractions (2025! divisible by all denominators).

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. Minimal ratio L/n is 6/11 (when 11|n) else 4/7 (7|n) else ≈2/3 (no small divisor). For M=3^{2025!}, M≡1 (mod p≤2025, p≠3). Thus M+4, M+1848374,… are odd, ≡5 (mod p) ⇒ only small divisor 5 (≠6). Hence their smallest admissible divisor ≥6 is huge → ratio≈2/3. M itself (c=0) has only 3‑factors ⇒ ratio 2/3 exactly. So g(0)=2/3, others≈2/3−δ with δ≈0 (since N·δ<1). Hence each floor(N·f/M)=⌊2N/3⌋ or ⌊2N/3⌋−1. Compute N=2025!; ⌊2N/3⌋ integer. Determine which c give −1 (if f/M<2/3). All c>0 give −1. So k₀=2N/3, k_i=2N/3−1 (i=1..5). Sum K=6·2N/3−5=4N−5. Then S=K/N=(4N−5)/N=4−5/N. Reduce: gcd(4N−5,N)=1 (since N odd, 5∤N). So p+q=(4N−5)+N=5N−5. Compute 5·2025!−5 mod 99991. Use factorial mod 99991 (prime) → (5·(2025! mod 99991)−5) mod 99991. This yields answer.

Insights: f(n)=n·min_{d|n}r(d) where r(d)=min LCM(a,b,c)/d. Global minima of r(d) (ordered): 6/11 (d≡0 mod 11), 4/7 (7), 10/17 (17), 20/31 (31), … For N=M+c (c even, N odd, N≡2 mod 3) only odd d coprime to 3 matter ⇒ d|c+1. Compute c+1 factorizations: 1848374+1=3²·5³·31·53 → best d=25 ⇒ r=16/25. 10162574+1=3²·5²·31²·47 → best d=47 ⇒ r=30/47. 265710644+1=3³·5·97·103·197 → best d=31 ⇒ r=20/31. 44636594+1=3·5·103·167·173 → best d=167 ⇒ r=110/167. For M (all 3‑powers) best d=9 ⇒ r=2/3; for 4M (5·3‑power) also r=2/3. Since each denominator ≤2025, 2025!·r is integer, so g(c)=r. Sum: 2/3+2/3+16/25+30/47+20/31+110/167 = 71453212/18248925. p+q≡10210 (mod 99991). Pitfalls: ignore even d (N odd), ensure d not multiple of 3, use smallest r‑giving divisor of c+1.
